answer.rationale: The most causally suggestive memory (b1, rollback cleared a checkout spike after a release) is off the table: compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so the release-correlation hypothesis cannot be acted on this window even though the 2h/90min timing points at it. That constraint reshapes the choice rather than resolving the diagnosis, so I keep the release as an unresolved suspected cause to hand to the next window. Of the remaining directions: enable_circuit_breaker (b4) fails fast by design, which sheds in-flight writes at settlement peak and directly violates 'without losing customer writes'; regional_failover (b2) worked in March but that was latency on a path where traffic could shift cleanly, whereas here writes are heavy and at peak, so a cross-region shift risks replication lag and dropped or duplicated settlement writes. That leaves relieving contention on the write primary. b5 is the closest structural match (read load stolen from the primary, write latency recovered), so I want its source record to confirm the mechanism was actually read/write contention on a shared primary and not an unrelated fix credited after the fact. I want b3 because it is the other candidate (add_capacity) and I suspect it does not transfer: it reads as headroom provisioned BEFORE a known peak, not capacity added mid-incident, and if that is what the archive says then add_capacity is a prevention lesson misfiled as a remediation lesson and cannot help in the next 90 minutes. Risk to flag downstream: shifting reads to replicas means anything reading those replicas sees stale data, so settlement dashboards, reconciliation, and any read-after-write check could quietly report wrong balances and be trusted as if authoritative; that must be labeled as replica-sourced, not treated as ledger truth. Hence a small guarded test: route a bounded slice of report/dashboard reads first, watch p99 on the write path and replica lag together, widen only if both hold. If the archive undercuts b5's mechanism, my fallback is a guarded, write-draining regional shift rather than the circuit breaker.
